newsitem.title: USA: Stock drop prompts calls to curb pollock catch.
newsitem.headline: Stock drop prompts calls to curb pollock catch.

text.p: The nation's biggest commercial seafood harvest is lated to shrink slightly next year, but not enough to satisfy critics who say stocks in the Bering Sea are disappearing too fast.

The North Pacific Fishery Management Council, the federal panel that manages commercial fishing in U.S. waters off Alaska, is eyeing a 1.13 million metric ton harvest cap for Alaskan pollock, a 5 percent reduction from the 1996 level.
A scientific panel recommended the cut, citing declines in the Bering Sea population.
The North Pacific council, meeting in Anchorage, is scheduled to set the 1997 harvest levels for pollock and other fish species by the end of the week.

But pointing to the estimated pollock biomass of 6 million metric tons -- down by about half from the level estimated in the mid-1980s -- environmentalistists say the 5 percent reduction is too small to protect the pollock and the species that feed on them.
The Alaska Marine Conservation Council recommends a 25 percent harvest cut, saying that could help prevent disasters that have occurred in fisheries elsewhere.
"If we look at the trends in fisheries that have crashed, usually nothing's done until they can't find any more fish," said Fran Bennis, project manager for the marine conservation group.
Bob Mikol, a board member of the group, accused the North Pacific council and the fishing industry of ignoring danger signs.
"They don't dispute that things are going downhill. They're trying to grab it before it's gone," said Mikol, a Sitka, Alaska, fisherman. "They know that it's swirling in the toilet already."
Greenpeace advocates an even deeper cut, of 35 percent to 40 percent.
Scientists for the National Marine Fisheries Service, which advises the North Pacific council, defended their 1.13 million metric ton recommendation as prudent.
"It's commensurate with the stock's ability to produce that amount," said Loh Lee Low, a NMFS scientist and member of the technical team that issued the harvest recommendation.
That harvest would take only about 16 percent to 18 percent of the Bering Sea's pollock, Low said.
"Right now we are exploiting at a very conservative exploitation rate," he said. "The question now is, are you going to impose additional safety beyond that? And I think that's a tough question."
There is no evidence that deeper cuts in the commercial harvest will boost the pollock stocks or the faltering populations of pollock-eating marine mammals and seabirds, Low said.
The fish, and their distribution by age group and location, are probably more affected by environmental factors such as ocean currents and temperatures, he said.
Industry members support the 1.13 million metric ton quota.
Paul MacGregor, head of the Seattle-based American Factory Trawler Association, said he trusts the scientists who monitor the Bering Sea fishery for the North Pacific council.
"They've done a pretty good job over the years," he said Thursday. "I'm not going to second-guess."

Alaskan pollock, the world's largest single-species commercial fish harvest, is used as fillets and in surimi, a paste formed into imitation shellfish. The harvest has been worth nearly $1 billion in some past years.
